cues.text: Section five: the VitalNet security and privacy hardening lab.
Let's begin with the scenario.
A regional triage nurse in Enugu should see only the necessary local patient information.
That nurse should also not have the authority to modify diagnostic notes.
So we are applying two ideas at once: limit what the nurse can see, and limit what the nurse can change.
The source gives us a demonstration in a PostgreSQL style, so let's walk through it.
The first thing to notice is the comment at the top.
It says to run this as an authorised administrator, in an isolated teaching database.
That matters, because these commands change permissions, and you should never practise them on a live system.
The first statement creates a role called triage underscore enugu, and it is marked NOLOGIN.
A role is a named bundle of permissions.
NOLOGIN means nobody can connect to the database directly as this role.
It exists only to hold permissions, and a real person would be given membership of it, or you would assume it for testing.
Next come two REVOKE ALL statements on the patient record table.
The first revokes all privileges from PUBLIC.
PUBLIC is a special pseudo-role meaning everyone, so this removes any blanket access that every user might otherwise have.
The second revokes all privileges on that table from triage underscore enugu itself.
Together, they start the role from a position of no direct access to the raw table.
Then we create a view named enugu underscore triage.
A view is a saved query that behaves like a virtual table.
This one selects three things from the patient record table.
First, the patient ID.

Second, a masked name: it takes the first letter of the patient's name, using the LEFT function with a length of one, and joins it, using the double vertical bar concatenation operator, to three asterisks.
So a name would show as its first letter followed by three stars.
This column is labelled masked underscore name.
Third, the triage status.
Finally, a WHERE clause restricts the rows to those where region equals Enugu.
So the view limits both the columns and the rows the nurse sees: no full name, no diagnostic notes, and only Enugu patients.
After that, GRANT SELECT on the enugu triage view is given to triage underscore enugu.
The role may read the view, and nothing more.
The comment that follows is a reminder: grant schema USAGE if required, and give membership of the role to a test login.
Without permission to use the schema, the role may not be able to reach the view at all, and without a test login, nobody can actually use the role.
Then the test.
The comment says to test the restricted role in an isolated session.
SET ROLE triage underscore enugu makes your current session act as that role.
SELECT star from enugu triage should then return only the masked, Enugu-only rows.
The comment after it states what we expect: a direct SELECT or UPDATE on patient record should fail, unless another inherited permission permits it.
That qualification is important.
If the role has inherited access from some other role, the direct access could still succeed.
Finally, RESET ROLE returns your session to your own identity.
Now the caution the source attaches to this example.
Views can expose approved columns and rows, but they do not revoke existing underlying access.
In other words, a view is not a lock.
If the user already has another route to the base table, the view does not close it.
So you must check several things: inherited roles, ownership, PUBLIC grants, SECURITY DEFINER functions, and any other access routes.
A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the privileges of its owner rather than its caller, so it can quietly open a path that you did not intend.
The source also notes that in PostgreSQL, row-level security can provide row restrictions.
But table owners, and roles with BYPASSRLS, may bypass the policies unless relevant safeguards apply.
The general advice is to use separate roles and to verify both the allowed actions and the denied actions.
Testing only that the permitted things work is not enough; you must prove the forbidden things fail.
Here is the row-level security example.
The first statement alters the patient record table to ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.
This turns on policy checking for the table.
The second creates a policy named enugu underscore only on patient record.
It applies FOR SELECT, so it governs reading, and TO triage underscore enugu, so it applies to that role.
The USING clause is the condition: region equals Enugu.
So when that role reads the table, only Enugu rows are visible.
The source then adds a warning.
A policy alone does not grant SELECT.
The policy filters rows, but the role still needs the privilege to select.
If you use direct table access, grant only the needed columns, and test how this interacts with the views.
The source also advises preferring an explicitly designed permission scheme rather than combining examples blindly.
Pasting the two snippets together without thinking could produce unexpected results.
Two final points.
Log access, but avoid storing raw sensitive information in the logs, since a log full of patient details becomes a new leak.
And remember that this lab is a synthetic illustration.
It is not a claim of full legal compliance.
